lessons.title: Definitions and exponential equations
lessons.summary: Build the six functions from exponentials and solve with a positive substitution.
lessons.objective: Use exponential definitions, reciprocal relations and all admissible roots.
lessons.before: Review exponentials, logarithms, quadratic equations and exact surds. In particular, an exponential of a real number is always positive.
lessons.ideas:
Two combinations of the same exponentials

\[\begin{gathered}\sinh x=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}2\\\cosh x=\frac{e^x+e^{-x}}2\\\tanh x=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}=\frac{e^{2x}-1}{e^{2x}+1}\end{gathered}\]

Sinh is odd, cosh is even, and cosh is positive for every real argument. The identity cosh²x−sinh²x=1 follows by subtracting the two squared definitions. Thus cosh x≥1. These functions are not periodic.

\[\begin{gathered}\operatorname{sech}x=\frac1{\cosh x}\\\operatorname{cosech}x=\frac1{\sinh x}\\\operatorname{coth}x=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x}\end{gathered}\]

Sech is defined for every real x. Cosech and coth exclude x=0 because sinh vanishes there. Inverse-function notation is introduced later; a reciprocal is a different operation.

A quadratic whose variable must be positive

\[\begin{gathered}A\cosh x+B\sinh x=C\\u=e^x>0\\(A+B)u^2-2Cu+(A-B)=0\end{gathered}\]

Multiplication by 2u is reversible because u is positive. Solve the polynomial, retain every positive root, then take its logarithm. A zero or negative polynomial root cannot represent eˣ. If A+B=0 the equation becomes linear in u; handle this parameter case separately.

A shifted cosh gives a minimum

For positive a,b, a eˣ+b e⁻ˣ equals 2√(ab) cosh(x−h), with h=½ln(b/a). Its minimum is 2√(ab), attained only at x=h. Keep the equality case when using this observation.
lessons.method:
1. State the definitions and any excluded arguments.
  2. Combine exponentials and set u=eˣ when useful.
  3. Handle a vanishing leading coefficient before applying a quadratic formula.
  4. Retain all positive u-values.
  5. Recover x by logarithms and check in the original relation.
mistakes: Hyperbolic functions are not periodic circular functions.
Cosh²x−sinh²x equals 1, with a minus sign.
Cosech and coth exclude zero.
The substitution u=eˣ requires u>0.
Do not divide away a factor that could be zero.

examples.title: 1 · Exact values without a calculator
examples.question: Find \(\sinh(\ln6)\), \(\cosh(\ln6)\) and \(\tanh(-\ln6)\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}e^{\ln6}=6,\qquad e^{-\ln6}=\frac16\\\sinh(\ln6)=\frac{35}{12}\\\cosh(\ln6)=\frac{37}{12}\\\tanh(-\ln6)=-\frac{35}{37}\end{gathered}\]

Use the difference and sum of the exponential pair, then form the ratio. Oddness determines the negative tanh value.

examples.title: 2 · Recover all reciprocal values
examples.question: Given \(\sinh a=\frac8{15}\) and \(a>0\), find cosh, tanh and the three reciprocal functions at a.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\cosh a=\sqrt{1+\frac{64}{225}}=\frac{17}{15}\\\tanh a=\frac8{17},\quad\operatorname{sech}a=\frac{15}{17}\\\operatorname{cosech}a=\frac{15}{8},\quad\operatorname{coth}a=\frac{17}{8}\end{gathered}\]

Cosh is positive, so the positive square root is compulsory. Take the reciprocals only after finding the correct ratios.

examples.title: 3 · Keep both logarithmic roots
examples.question: Solve \(6\cosh x-4\sinh x=7\) for every real x.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}e^x+5e^{-x}=7\\u=e^x>0:\quad u^2-7u+5=0\\u=\frac{7\pm\sqrt{29}}2\\x=\ln\left(\frac{7+\sqrt{29}}2\right)\\ x=\ln\left(\frac{7-\sqrt{29}}2\right)\end{gathered}\]

Both u-roots are positive because √29<7. Each gives one real x; neither may be discarded.

examples.title: 4 · Read a minimum from a shifted function
examples.question: Find the minimum of \(5e^x+20e^{-x}\), and solve \(5e^x+20e^{-x}=25\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}5e^x+20e^{-x}=20\cosh(x-\ln2)\\\min=20\quad\text{at }x=\ln2\\\cosh(x-\ln2)=\frac54\\x=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=\ln4\end{gathered}\]

The shift locates the minimum. Cosh takes the value 5/4 at the two arguments ±ln2, so both intersections are needed.

lessons.title: Graphs, ranges and transformations
lessons.summary: Track support, symmetry and unattained asymptotic values.
lessons.objective: Describe transformed hyperbolic graphs and determine exact graph features.
lessons.before: Complete definitions. Review translations, stretches, reflections and open or closed interval endpoints.
lessons.ideas:
Shape and real ranges

Sinh increases through the origin with all-real domain and range. Cosh is U-shaped, symmetric about the vertical axis, and has minimum 1. Tanh increases between horizontal asymptotes −1 and 1, neither of which it reaches. Sech is positive with maximum 1 and tends to zero in both tails. Cosech is odd with vertical asymptote x=0 and horizontal asymptote y=0. Coth is odd, excludes x=0, and has horizontal asymptotes ±1.

\[\begin{gathered}\operatorname{range}(\cosh)=[1,\infty)\\\operatorname{range}(\tanh)=(-1,1)\\\operatorname{range}(\operatorname{sech})=(0,1]\\\operatorname{range}(\operatorname{cosech})=(-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)\\\operatorname{range}(\operatorname{coth})=(-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty)\end{gathered}\]

Transform the input first

For y=A f(B(x−h))+D, a base point (r,s) maps to (h+r/B,D+As). Negative A reflects vertically; negative B reflects horizontally. A finite turning point is attained and included in the range. A finite horizontal asymptote is a limit and may remain excluded.

Describe the whole sketch

State the domain, range, exact intercepts, symmetry and asymptotes. Solve the argument equation to locate a vertical asymptote. Check the sign on each side instead of drawing a branch through an excluded input. A flat-looking inverse-sinh tail is not a horizontal asymptote.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the base function and its real domain.
  2. Map important points and symmetry under the transformation.
  3. Calculate asymptotes by limits and excluded arguments.
  4. Solve for all intercepts with exact values.
  5. State the range with correct endpoint inclusion.
mistakes: A shifted vertical asymptote is found from the argument, not from y=0.
Horizontal asymptotes of tanh and coth are not attained.
A negative multiplier reverses graph direction.
Sech reaches 1 but never reaches 0.
Do not join branches across a forbidden input.

examples.title: 1 · A reflected sine-hyperbolic curve
examples.question: Describe \(y=1-3\sinh(x+2)\): symmetry, direction, range and horizontal intercept.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\text{centre}=(-2,1)\\\text{domain}=\mathbb R,\qquad\text{range}=\mathbb R\\\sinh(x+2)=\frac13\\x=\ln\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{10}}3\right)-2\end{gathered}\]

The vertical reflection makes the curve decrease. Its central point shifts left by 2 and up by 1. There are no horizontal or vertical asymptotes.

examples.title: 2 · A cosh minimum and two zeros
examples.question: Describe the minimum, range and zeros of \(y=2\cosh(2x-2)-3\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\text{minimum point}=(1,-1)\\\text{range}=[-1,\infty)\\\cosh(2x-2)=\frac32\\x=1\pm\frac12\ln\left(\frac{3+\sqrt5}2\right)\end{gathered}\]

The argument vanishes at x=1. The positive multiplier keeps this a minimum. The two zeros lie symmetrically on opposite sides of x=1.

examples.title: 3 · A decreasing bounded curve
examples.question: Find the range, asymptotes and centre of \(y=4-2\tanh(x-3)\). Does it cross the horizontal axis?
examples.solution: \[\begin{gathered}-1<\tanh(x-3)<1\\2The curve decreases from values near 6 to values near 2. Neither endpoint is attained, and y is always positive, so there is no horizontal-axis intersection.

examples.title: 4 · Move a reciprocal singularity
examples.question: Find the domain, range, asymptotes and zero of \(y=\operatorname{coth}(2x-1)+2\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x\ne\frac12\\\text{range}=(-\infty,1)\cup(3,\infty)\\\text{asymptotes: }x=\frac12,\ y=1,\ y=3\\\operatorname{coth}(2x-1)=-2\\x=\frac12-\frac14\ln3\end{gathered}\]

The zero lies on the branch to the left of the vertical asymptote. The lower branch ends towards y=1; the upper branch tends towards y=3.

lessons.title: Identities and admissible solutions
lessons.summary: Prove identities from definitions, then preserve all permitted branches.
lessons.objective: Derive and use hyperbolic identities with the restrictions needed for equivalence.
lessons.before: Complete graphs and ranges. Review expanding powers and solving polynomial equations.
lessons.ideas:
Prove a general statement before substituting numbers

Replace the functions by their exponential definitions, expand one side, and simplify towards the other. State restrictions when a denominator can vanish. A numerical example can check an identity, but is not its proof.

\[\begin{gathered}\sinh(u+v)=\sinh u\cosh v+\cosh u\sinh v\\\cosh(u+v)=\cosh u\cosh v+\sinh u\sinh v\\\sinh2x=2\sinh x\cosh x\\\cosh2x=2\cosh^2x-1=1+2\sinh^2x\\\tanh2x=\frac{2\tanh x}{1+\tanh^2x}\end{gathered}\]

Polynomial roots need function ranges

If s=sinh x, then every real s is allowed and gives exactly one x. If c=cosh x, require c≥1; c=1 gives x=0, while c>1 gives two opposite roots. If t=tanh x, require −1<t<1. Do not divide by s or t before considering its zero value.

Count horizontal intersections

A discriminant counts polynomial roots before these restrictions. To classify a parameter problem, first identify the admissible variable range and boundary values. Include equality cases separately.
lessons.method:
1. Choose exponential definitions or a proved identity.
  2. Record every denominator restriction.
  3. Substitute s=sinh x, c=cosh x or t=tanh x with its range.
  4. Solve and discard only inadmissible substituted roots.
  5. Recover all corresponding x-values, including zero and both cosh branches.
mistakes: Hyperbolic addition formulae have different signs from circular identities.
Keep the zero root before cancelling a factor.
A real quadratic root below 1 cannot be cosh x.
A small discriminant does not count admissible x-roots.
Restrictions belong to the original expression as well as the simplified one.

examples.title: 1 · Establish the double-angle formula
examples.question: Prove \(\sinh2x=2\sinh x\cosh x\) from exponential definitions.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}2\sinh x\cosh x=\frac{(e^x-e^{-x})(e^x+e^{-x})}{2}\\=\frac{e^{2x}-e^{-2x}}2=\sinh2x\end{gathered}\]

The cross terms cancel. No division was needed, so the result holds for every real x, including zero.

examples.title: 2 · A root that cancellation would lose
examples.question: Solve \(\tanh2x=\frac85\tanh x\).
examples.solution: \[\begin{gathered}t=\tanh x,\quad -1The denominator is positive. All three substituted values lie in the tanh range, and each corresponds to one real x.

examples.title: 3 · A triple angle with two branches
examples.question: Use \(\cosh3x=4\cosh^3x-3\cosh x\) to solve \(\cosh3x=13\cosh x\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}4\cosh x(\cosh^2x-4)=0\\\cosh x=2\\x=\pm\ln(2+\sqrt3)\end{gathered}\]

Cosh is positive, so its factor cannot vanish. The negative candidate −2 is outside its range; the positive value 2 gives two opposite x-values.

examples.title: 4 · An identity locates a minimum
examples.question: Write \(25\cosh x-7\sinh x\) as a shifted cosh and find its minimum.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}R^2=25^2-7^2=576,\qquad R=24\\\cosh b=\frac{25}{24},\quad\sinh b=\frac7{24}\\e^b=\frac43,\quad b=\ln\frac43\\25\cosh x-7\sinh x=24\cosh\left(x-\ln\frac43\right)\end{gathered}\]

The minimum is 24, attained only at x=ln(4/3). Matching both exponential coefficients verifies the shift, rather than just matching the minimum.

lessons.title: Inverse functions and principal branches
lessons.summary: An inverse undoes a one-to-one function; it is not a reciprocal.
lessons.objective: Find inverse formulae, domains and ranges using the correct principal branch.
lessons.before: Complete identities. Review one-to-one restrictions and reflection in y=x.
lessons.ideas:
Three standard real inverses

\[\begin{gathered}\sinh:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R\\\cosh:[0,\infty)\longrightarrow[1,\infty)\\\tanh:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-1,1)\end{gathered}\]

Sinh and tanh are already one-to-one. Cosh needs a restriction; its principal inverse returns a non-negative value. The inverse domain equals the restricted function's range, and the inverse range equals its restricted domain.

\[\begin{gathered}\sinh^{-1}(\sinh x)=x\\\tanh^{-1}(\tanh x)=x\\\cosh^{-1}(\cosh x)=|x|\end{gathered}\]

The reverse compositions require the input to lie in the inverse domain. The notation sinh⁻¹x means inverse sinh, not 1/sinh x. Reciprocals retain the names cosech, sech and coth.

Transformed inverse functions

Write y=f(x), isolate the base hyperbolic function and impose its branch before inverting. Interchange variable names only at the end. Keep all affine shifts and stretches. Reflection in y=x exchanges horizontal and vertical graph features.
lessons.method:
1. Specify a one-to-one branch for the original function.
  2. Find its exact range.
  3. Rearrange y=f(x) and apply the principal inverse.
  4. Interchange names to obtain f⁻¹.
  5. State inverse domain and range and test the requested values.
mistakes: Inverse notation and reciprocal notation have different meanings.
Principal inverse cosh has a non-negative output.
Cosh⁻¹(cosh x) equals |x|, not x everywhere.
The inverse domain is the original range.
Carry every affine transformation through the inversion.

examples.title: 1 · Choose the least increasing branch
examples.question: Restrict \(f(x)=\cosh(4x-3)\) to an increasing branch, then find its inverse and both inverse intervals.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x\ge\frac34\\f^{-1}(x)=\frac{\cosh^{-1}x+3}{4}\\\operatorname{domain}(f^{-1})=[1,\infty)\\\operatorname{range}(f^{-1})=[3/4,\infty)\end{gathered}\]

The argument is non-negative precisely on this branch. Applying inverse cosh there produces 4x−3 directly, with no ± sign.

examples.title: 2 · Invert a bounded transformed function
examples.question: For \(f(x)=5\tanh(x-2)-3\), find the inverse, its domain and its range.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}y+3=5\tanh(x-2)\\x=2+\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{y+3}{5}\right)\\f^{-1}(x)=2+\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+3}{5}\right)\\\operatorname{domain}(f^{-1})=(-8,2)\\\operatorname{range}(f^{-1})=\mathbb R\end{gathered}\]

The original output lies strictly between −8 and 2, so neither endpoint is admitted to the inverse domain.

examples.title: 3 · The modulus determines both roots
examples.question: Solve \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh(3x+4))=2\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}|3x+4|=2\\3x+4=2\quad\text{or}\quad3x+4=-2\\x=-\frac23\quad\text{or}\quad x=-2\end{gathered}\]

Both signs are needed because principal inverse cosh returns the magnitude of the inner real argument. Substitution confirms both roots.

examples.title: 4 · Compose in the permitted direction
examples.question: Simplify \(\cosh(\sinh^{-1}z)\) and \(\tanh(\sinh^{-1}z)\), then solve the second expression equal to \(\frac5{13}\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\cosh(\sinh^{-1}z)=\sqrt{1+z^2}\\\tanh(\sinh^{-1}z)=\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+z^2}}\\144z^2=25,\qquad z>0\\z=\frac5{12}\end{gathered}\]

The positive square root is forced by cosh. The original equation fixes a positive sign, so the negative root introduced by squaring is rejected.

lessons.title: Logarithmic forms and exact equations
lessons.summary: Derive a formula and justify the branch and domain at the same time.
lessons.objective: Derive the three main logarithmic inverse forms and solve equations without extraneous roots.
lessons.before: Complete inverse functions. Review quadratic roots, logarithm laws and their positive arguments.
lessons.ideas:
Solve for a positive exponential

To derive an inverse formula, set y equal to the inverse and write the corresponding forward relation. Substituting u=eʸ turns the exponential relation into a quadratic or linear equation. Select u>0 and, for inverse cosh, u≥1.

\[\begin{gathered}\sinh^{-1}x=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right),\quad x\in\mathbb R\\\cosh^{-1}x=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right),\quad x\ge1\\\tanh^{-1}x=\frac12\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x},\quad -1For inverse sinh, √(x²+1)>|x| makes the plus root positive for every real input. For inverse cosh, the plus root is at least 1 and gives the non-negative principal output. For inverse tanh, the quotient must be positive on its real inverse domain.

Reciprocal inverses follow from the same functions

\[\begin{gathered}\operatorname{coth}^{-1}x=\tanh^{-1}(1/x),\quad |x|>1\\\operatorname{sech}^{-1}x=\cosh^{-1}(1/x),\quad 0Here inverse sech uses the non-negative branch. The reciprocal inside an inverse does not turn inverse notation into reciprocal notation.

Preserve equivalence in an equation

Intersect all real domains before combining logarithms, squaring or applying a forward function. Cosh is one-to-one only on a restricted half-line. At the end check every candidate in the original domain; a valid polynomial root may still be invalid for an inverse expression.
lessons.method:
1. Write the original real domain.
  2. Use the exponential definition or a justified logarithmic inverse form.
  3. Keep positive logarithm arguments and the required principal branch.
  4. Solve the algebraic equation.
  5. Retain every candidate in the original domain and check it.
mistakes: The logarithm requires a positive argument.
Inverse cosh chooses a non-negative output.
Combining inverse tanh terms needs the intersection of their domains.
Squaring can introduce the wrong sign.
Do not present a reciprocal as an inverse function.

examples.title: 1 · Derive inverse sinh for every real input
examples.question: Derive a logarithmic expression for \(\sinh^{-1}x\), with its real domain.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x=\sinh y,\quad u=e^y>0\\u^2-2xu-1=0\\u=x\pm\sqrt{x^2+1}\\\sinh^{-1}x=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)\end{gathered}\]

The minus root is negative because √(x²+1)>|x|. The plus root is strictly positive for every real x, so the displayed formula has all-real domain.

examples.title: 2 · Derive inverse cosh on its principal branch
examples.question: Derive the logarithmic expression for principal \(\cosh^{-1}x\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x=\cosh y,\quad y\ge0,\quad u=e^y\ge1\\u^2-2xu+1=0\\u=x\pm\sqrt{x^2-1}\\\cosh^{-1}x=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right),\quad x\ge1\end{gathered}\]

For x>1 the two roots are positive reciprocals. Only the plus root is at least 1, as the principal branch requires. At x=1 both roots equal 1 and y=0.

examples.title: 3 · Derive inverse tanh and its open domain
examples.question: Derive a logarithmic expression for \(\tanh^{-1}x\).
examples.solution: \[\begin{gathered}x=\frac{e^{2y}-1}{e^{2y}+1}\\e^{2y}=\frac{1+x}{1-x}\\\tanh^{-1}x=\frac12\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x},\quad -1The real inverse domain comes from the open range of tanh. The two endpoints would make the logarithm invalid or unbounded, and are excluded.

examples.title: 4 · Reject a root outside both inverse domains
examples.question: Solve \(\tanh^{-1}x+\tanh^{-1}(3x)=\frac12\ln7\).
examples.solution: \[\begin{gathered}-\frac13Only the smaller root lies in the common domain. All logarithm arguments are positive there, so the transformations are reversible and this is the complete solution.

lessons.title: Mixed problems and later-topic extensions
lessons.summary: Classify core equations completely; attempt extensions only after their prerequisites.
lessons.objective: Combine range restrictions, parameter cases and principal branches, then review optional later-topic applications.
lessons.before: Complete all five preceding lessons. Questions 41–45 are chapter-core review. Questions 46–50 are later-topic extensions: attempt them after differentiation, integration and first-order differential equations. The last two worked examples also need these later prerequisites.
lessons.ideas:
A parameter changes the shape and the number of roots

In A cosh x−b sinh x=k, the cases |b|<A, |b|=A and |b|>A behave differently when A>0. The first case has a positive minimum and up to two roots. Equality leaves a single positive exponential. In the last case the exponential coefficients have opposite signs, giving a strictly monotone function with all-real range.

Substitutions carry ranges with them

\[\begin{gathered}c=\cosh x\ge1,\qquad s=\sinh x\in\mathbb R\\t=\tanh(x/2)\in(-1,1)\\\sinh x=\frac{2t}{1-t^2},\qquad\cosh x=\frac{1+t^2}{1-t^2}\end{gathered}\]

Positive x corresponds to positive sinh x. A repeated polynomial root gives one distinct substituted value, whose corresponding x-values still depend on the function. For radical inverse equations, keep the non-negative branches before applying cosh.

Later-topic extension: verify a proposed solution

After learning integration and differential equations, a hyperbolic integrating factor can simplify a linear equation. Substitute the final expression into the original equation, check the initial condition and state the interval where the steps are valid. An endpoint limit need not be a solution through that endpoint.
lessons.method:
1. Identify whether the task is core review or a later-topic extension.
  2. Record the domain and every special parameter case.
  3. Use a range-preserving substitution or principal inverse.
  4. Count all distinct real roots, including equality boundaries.
  5. For an extension, verify the differential equation, initial value and stated interval.
mistakes: A discriminant does not impose the range c≥1.
Special parameters can turn a quadratic into a linear equation.
A positive x-root needs a positive sinh x-value.
Applying cosh is not globally one-to-one.
Later-topic differential equations require their own prerequisites and domain checks.

examples.title: 1 · Include the exponential boundary cases
examples.question: For real a, classify the number of real roots of \(2\cosh x-a\sinh x=k\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}|a|<2:\quad \min=\sqrt{4-a^2}\\|a|=2:\quad F(x)=2e^x\ \text{or}\ 2e^{-x}\\|a|>2:\quad \operatorname{range}(F)=\mathbb R\end{gathered}\]

For |a|<2 there are zero, one or two roots as k is below, equal to or above the minimum. For |a|=2 there is one root for k>0 and none otherwise. For |a|>2 the function is strictly monotone and gives exactly one root for each real k.

examples.title: 2 · An inverse equation with a radical
examples.question: Solve \(\cosh^{-1}(2x+5)=2\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{3x}\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x\ge0\\2x+5=\cosh\left(2\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{3x}\right)=1+6x\\x=1\end{gathered}\]

Both original sides are non-negative on the common domain. Cosh is one-to-one there, so the transformation is reversible. The candidate x=1 satisfies the original equation and is unique.

examples.title: 3 · Extension after first-order differential equations
examples.question: After the later prerequisites, solve \(y^\prime+2y\tanh x=1\), with \(y(0)=3\), and find the limit as x→∞.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mu(x)=\cosh^2x\\(y\cosh^2x)^\prime=\cosh^2x\\y=\frac{\frac x2+\frac14\sinh2x+3}{\cosh^2x}\\\lim_{x\to\infty}y=\frac12\end{gathered}\]

The integrating factor is positive everywhere. The initial value sets the constant to 3. Rewriting the sinh term as ½tanh x shows the limit; the remaining linear term decays after multiplication by sech²x.

examples.title: 4 · Extension with an explicit interval
examples.question: For x>−4, solve \((x+4)y^\prime-y=(x+4)^2\sinh^{-1}((x+4)/2)\), with \(y(0)=0\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}u=x+4,\qquad v=\sinh^{-1}(u/2)\\\left(\frac yu\right)^\prime=\sinh^{-1}(u/2)\\\frac yu=uv-\sqrt{u^2+4}+C\\C=2\sqrt5-4\sinh^{-1}2\end{gathered}\]

Here u=x+4, so du/dx=1. Multiply the final right-hand side by u to obtain y explicitly. Integration by parts supplies the displayed antiderivative. Differentiating y/u verifies the equation; at x=0 the bracket is zero. The restriction x>−4 keeps the integrating-factor step valid.

questions.title: Exact values from exponential definitions
questions.prompt_html:
1. Use exponential definitions to find the exact values of \(\sinh(\ln4)\), \(\cosh(\ln4)\) and \(\tanh(-\ln4)\).

    [3]

  2. Prove directly from the definitions that \((\cosh x+\sinh x)(\cosh x-\sinh x)=1\) for every real \(x\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\frac{15}{8},\ \frac{17}{8},\ -\frac{15}{17}\), respectively.

(b)

\(\cosh x+\sinh x=e^x\) and \(\cosh x-\sinh x=e^{-x}\), so their product is 1.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The definitions give

\[\sinh(\ln4)=\frac{4-\frac14}{2}=\frac{15}{8},\qquad \cosh(\ln4)=\frac{4+\frac14}{2}=\frac{17}{8}.\]

For the negative argument, interchange the two exponentials in the numerator of sinh; cosh is unchanged. Thus

\[\tanh(-\ln4)=\frac{-15/8}{17/8}=-\frac{15}{17}.\]

(b)

Adding and subtracting the exponential definitions gives

\[\cosh x+\sinh x=e^x,\qquad \cosh x-\sinh x=e^{-x}.\]

Their product is \(e^xe^{-x}=1\). Both definitions are valid for every real \(x\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(e^{\ln4}=4\) and \(e^{-\ln4}=\frac14\).

(b)

Simplify the two factors separately.

questions.title: Recovering the hyperbolic ratios
questions.prompt_html:
It is given that \(a>0\) and \(\tanh a=\frac5{13}\).

  1. Find the exact values of \(\sinh a,\cosh a,\operatorname{sech}a,\operatorname{cosech}a\) and \(\operatorname{coth}a\).

    [4]

  2. Hence find \(a\) in logarithmic form.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(\sinh a=5u\) and \(\cosh a=13u\). Since cosh is positive, \(u>0\). The identity yields

\[(13u)^2-(5u)^2=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad144u^2=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=\frac1{12}.\]

Hence \(\sinh a=5/12\) and \(\cosh a=13/12\). Taking the reciprocals of cosh, sinh and tanh gives \(12/13\), \(12/5\) and \(13/5\), respectively.

(b)

\[e^a=\frac{13}{12}+\frac5{12}=\frac32.\]

Taking logarithms gives \(a=\ln(3/2)>0\), consistent with the condition.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Write \(\sinh a=5u\), \(\cosh a=13u\), and use \(\cosh^2a-\sinh^2a=1\).

(b)

Use \(e^a=\cosh a+\sinh a\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the fundamental identity with the given ratio.

questions.title: An equation and an inequality
questions.prompt_html:
1. Solve \(3\cosh x-2\sinh x=3\), giving all real solutions in exact form.

    [4]

  2. Solve \(3\cosh x-2\sinh x<3\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Using exponentials,

\[3\cosh x-2\sinh x=\frac{e^x+5e^{-x}}2.\]

Put \(u=e^x>0\). Multiplying by \(2u\) gives

\[u^2-6u+5=(u-1)(u-5)=0.\]

Both values of \(u\) are positive, so both are allowed. Therefore \(x=0\) or \(x=\ln5\).

(b)

The inequality is equivalent to \((u-1)(u-5)<0\), because multiplying by \(2u>0\) preserves its direction. Thus \(1<u<5\). Since the logarithm is increasing,

\[0<x<\ln5.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Set \(u=e^x>0\).

(b)

The multiplier \(2e^x\) is always positive.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use exponential definitions and a positive substitution.

questions.title: A ratio that simplifies
questions.prompt_html:
1. Starting from exponential definitions, show that \(\frac{\sinh 2x}{\cosh x}=e^x-e^{-x}\).

    [3]

  2. Hence solve \(\sinh2x=3\cosh x\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{\sinh2x}{\cosh x}=\frac{e^{2x}-e^{-2x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}=\frac{(e^x-e^{-x})(e^x+e^{-x})}{e^x+e^{-x}}=e^x-e^{-x}.\]

The cancelled factor is strictly positive, so the identity is valid for all real \(x\).

(b)

As \(\cosh x>0\), division loses no solutions. Part (a) gives \(e^x-e^{-x}=3\). With \(u=e^x>0\),

\[u^2-3u-1=0,\qquad u=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{13}}2.\]

Only the positive root is admissible. Thus \(x=\ln((3+\sqrt{13})/2)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor \(e^{2x}-e^{-2x}\).

(b)

Use the identity, then solve a quadratic in \(e^x\).

questions.title: Opposite exponential factors
questions.prompt_html:
A real number \(x\) satisfies \(\cosh x+\sinh x=7(\cosh x-\sinh x)\).

  1. Find \(x\) exactly.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact values of \(\tanh x\) and \(\tanh2x\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The two brackets are \(e^x\) and \(e^{-x}\). Therefore

\[e^x=7e^{-x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{2x}=7\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\frac12\ln7.\]

(b)

From \(e^{2x}=7\),

\[\tanh x=\frac{7-1}{7+1}=\frac34.\]

Also \(e^{4x}=49\), so

\[\tanh2x=\frac{49-1}{49+1}=\frac{24}{25}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Simplify each bracket using exponential definitions.

(b)

Use \(\tanh z=(e^{2z}-1)/(e^{2z}+1)\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain an equation in e to the 2x.
Use a correct exponential expression for tanh.

questions.title: A minimum without differentiation
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=2e^x+8e^{-x}\), for \(x\in\mathbb R\).

  1. Write \(f(x)\) in the form \(A\cosh(x-b)\), where \(A>0\).

    [3]

  2. State the minimum value of \(f\) and where it occurs.

    [1]

  3. Solve \(f(x)=10\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[A\cosh(x-b)=\frac{Ae^{-b}}2e^x+\frac{Ae^b}2e^{-x}.\]

Matching coefficients gives \(Ae^{-b}=4\) and \(Ae^b=16\). Multiplication gives \(A^2=64\), so \(A=8\). Then \(e^b=2\), so \(b=\ln2\).

(b)

Since \(\cosh u\ge1\), with equality only at \(u=0\), the minimum is \(8\), attained at \(x=\ln2\).

(c)

The equation becomes \(\cosh(x-\ln2)=5/4\). Thus \(x-\ln2=\pm\ln2\), giving \(x=0\) or \(x=\ln4\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Compare the coefficients of \(e^x\) and \(e^{-x}\).

(b)

The least value of cosh is 1.

(c)

Use \(\cosh(\ln2)=5/4\).

questions.title: The sum of two logarithmic roots
questions.prompt_html:
1. Solve \(4\cosh x+\sinh x=7\), giving both answers in logarithmic form.

    [4]

  2. Without approximating either root, find their sum and determine its sign.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(u=e^x>0\). Then

\[\frac{5u+3/u}{2}=7\quad\Longrightarrow\quad5u^2-14u+3=0.\]

The roots are \(u=(7\pm\sqrt{34})/5\). Both are positive because \(7>\sqrt{34}\). Taking logarithms gives the stated two values.

(b)

If the roots in \(x\) are \(x_1,x_2\), then

\[x_1+x_2=\ln(e^{x_1}e^{x_2})=\ln\frac35.\]

This is negative since \(0<3/5<1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The exponential equation has two positive roots.

(b)

The product of the two exponential roots is \(3/5\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the product of the exponential roots.

questions.title: A parameter and an open range
questions.prompt_html:
Define \(f(x)=\frac{e^{-x}}{\cosh x}\), for real \(x\).

  1. Show that \(f(x)=1-\tanh x\), and state its range.

    [3]

  2. Find all real values of \(k\) for which \(f(x)=k\) has a real solution, and find that solution in terms of \(k\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(f(x)=1-\tanh x\), with range \((0,2)\).

(b)

\(0<k<2\), with the unique solution \(x=\frac12\ln\frac{2-k}{k}\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Dividing \(e^{-x}=\cosh x-\sinh x\) by the positive number \(\cosh x\) gives \(f(x)=1-\tanh x\). Since \(-1<\tanh x<1\), the range is \(0<f(x)<2\). Neither endpoint is attained.

(b)

\[f(x)=\frac{2}{1+e^{2x}}=k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{2x}=\frac{2-k}{k}.\]

The right-hand side is positive exactly when \(0<k<2\). For each such \(k\), the exponential equation has one real solution,

\[x=\frac12\ln\frac{2-k}{k}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Write \(e^{-x}=\cosh x-\sinh x\).

(b)

Use \(f(x)=2/(1+e^{2x})\).

questions.title: A translated hyperbolic sine graph
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation \(y=\sinh(2x)-1\).

  1. Sketch \(C\). State its domain and range, label both axis intercepts in exact form, and identify its centre of symmetry.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Domain and range: \(\mathbb R\). Intercepts \((0,-1)\) and \((\tfrac12\ln(1+\sqrt2),0)\). Centre \((0,-1)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The function \(\sinh(2x)\) is odd, continuous and strictly increasing, with all real values. Subtracting 1 gives centre of symmetry \((0,-1)\), while the domain and range remain \(\mathbb R\).

At \(x=0\), \(y=-1\). For the horizontal-axis intercept,

\[\sinh(2x)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2x=\ln(1+\sqrt2).\]

The sketch is an increasing S-shaped curve through these intercepts. It has no horizontal or vertical asymptote.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Apply a horizontal compression and a vertical translation to \(y=\sinh x\).

questions.title: A shifted hyperbolic cosine graph
questions.prompt_html:
A curve has equation \(y=3\cosh(x+\ln2)-4\).

  1. Sketch the curve, stating its minimum point, its range and all axis intercepts in exact form.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The argument of cosh is zero at \(x=-\ln2\), where \(y=3-4=-1\). Thus the curve is symmetric about \(x=-\ln2\), and its range is \([-1,\infty)\).

At \(x=0\), \(\cosh(\ln2)=5/4\), so \(y=-1/4\). Horizontal-axis intersections satisfy

\[\cosh(x+\ln2)=\frac43.\]

There are two arguments, \(\pm\cosh^{-1}(4/3)\), giving

\[x=-\ln2\pm\ln\frac{4+\sqrt7}{3}.\]

Both arms of the U-shaped curve rise without bound.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The minimum occurs when the argument of cosh is zero.

questions.title: Asymptotes of a transformed tanh curve
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(y=2\tanh(3x)-1\).

  1. Sketch the curve. State the domain, range and equations of the asymptotes, and find both axis intercepts.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

As \(x\to-\infty\), \(\tanh(3x)\to-1\), so \(y\to-3\). As \(x\to\infty\), \(y\to1\). These limiting values are not attained, giving range \((-3,1)\); the domain is \(\mathbb R\).

The vertical-axis intercept is \((0,-1)\). For the horizontal-axis intercept,

\[\tanh(3x)=\frac12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad3x=\frac12\ln3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\frac16\ln3.\]

The graph increases between its two horizontal asymptotes and is centrally symmetric about \((0,-1)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The limits of tanh at the two ends of the real line are different.

questions.title: A reciprocal graph and an inequality
questions.prompt_html:
The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=\operatorname{sech}(x-1)\).

  1. Sketch the graph. State its range, maximum point and any asymptotes.

    [3]

  2. Solve \(g(x)\ge\frac12\), giving exact endpoints.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(\cosh(x-1)\ge1\), its reciprocal lies in \((0,1]\). Equality \(g=1\) occurs at \(x=1\). The graph is positive and symmetric about \(x=1\), and tends to zero at both ends. There are no vertical asymptotes or horizontal-axis intercepts.

(b)

Because cosh is positive,

\[\frac1{\cosh(x-1)}\ge\frac12\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\cosh(x-1)\le2.\]

By symmetry and monotonicity of cosh on \([0,\infty)\), \(|x-1|\le\cosh^{-1}2=\ln(2+\sqrt3)\). Hence the required closed interval is as stated.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\operatorname{sech}u=1/\cosh u\).

(b)

Invert the inequality using the positivity of cosh.

questions.title: Hyperbolic cosecant
questions.prompt_html:
A curve has equation \(y=\operatorname{cosech}(2x)\).

  1. Sketch the curve, stating its domain, range, symmetry and asymptotes.

    [3]

  2. Find the point on the curve whose \(y\)-coordinate is \(-\frac43\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Domain and range \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\); odd symmetry; asymptotes \(x=0\), \(y=0\).

(b)

\(\left(-\frac12\ln2,-\frac43\right)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The denominator \(\sinh(2x)\) vanishes only at \(x=0\), so that value is excluded and \(x=0\) is a vertical asymptote. The reciprocal is never zero, but tends to zero as \(|x|\to\infty\); thus \(y=0\) is a horizontal asymptote. The graph is odd, with one positive branch for \(x>0\) and one negative branch for \(x<0\). Each nonzero real output occurs.

(b)

\[\operatorname{cosech}(2x)=-\frac43\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sinh(2x)=-\frac34.\]

Since \(\sinh(\ln2)=3/4\) and sinh is odd and one-to-one, \(2x=-\ln2\). Therefore the point is \((-\tfrac12\ln2,-4/3)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take the reciprocal of sinh, keeping its sign.

(b)

The corresponding sinh value is the reciprocal of \(-4/3\).

questions.title: A displaced coth curve
questions.prompt_html:
The curve \(C\) has equation \(y=\operatorname{coth}(x+\ln2)\).

  1. Sketch \(C\). State its domain, range, asymptotes and vertical-axis intercept.

    [4]

  2. Solve \(\operatorname{coth}(x+\ln2)=2\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The denominator vanishes when \(x+\ln2=0\), giving vertical asymptote \(x=-\ln2\). On the right branch coth decreases from \(+\infty\) towards 1; on the left it decreases from values near \(-1\) towards \(-\infty\). The horizontal asymptotes are \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\), neither attained.

At \(x=0\),

\[\operatorname{coth}(\ln2)=\frac{5/4}{3/4}=\frac53.\]

The two stated intervals form the range.

(b)

With \(u=x+\ln2\),

\[\frac{e^{2u}+1}{e^{2u}-1}=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^{2u}=3.\]

Thus \(u=\tfrac12\ln3>0\), and \(x=\tfrac12\ln3-\ln2\). This lies to the right of the vertical asymptote.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The pole of coth moves with its argument; its limiting values remain unchanged.

(b)

Use the exponential definition of coth.

questions.title: An absolute value and the number of intersections
questions.prompt_html:
The function \(h(x)=|\sinh x|-1\) is defined for all real \(x\).

  1. Sketch \(y=h(x)\), marking its minimum point and axis intercepts.

    [3]

  2. For each real \(k\), state the number of distinct solutions of \(h(x)=k\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Minimum \((0,-1)\); zeros \(x=\pm\ln(1+\sqrt2)\); even symmetry.

(b)

No solutions if \(k<-1\); one if \(k=-1\); two if \(k>-1\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The graph of \(|\sinh x|\) is even and is zero only at \(x=0\). Therefore \(h\) has minimum \(-1\) there, and is symmetric about the vertical axis. Its two branches meet in a corner at \((0,-1)\). The horizontal-axis intercepts satisfy \(|\sinh x|=1\), hence \(x=\pm\ln(1+\sqrt2)\).

(b)

The equation is \(|\sinh x|=k+1\). A negative right-hand side is impossible. If it is zero, \(x=0\) is the only solution. If it is positive, sinh being odd and strictly increasing gives exactly one positive and one negative solution. This proves all three cases, including the boundary.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

First reflect the negative part of sinh above the horizontal axis, then translate down.

(b)

Compare the horizontal line with the minimum height.

questions.title: Reconstructing a hyperbolic graph
questions.prompt_html:
A curve has equation \(y=A\tanh(B(x-h))+D\), where \(A>0\) and \(B>0\). Its horizontal asymptotes are \(y=-2\) and \(y=6\), its centre of symmetry is \((1,2)\), and it passes through \(\left(1+\frac12\ln3,\frac{26}{5}\right)\).

  1. Find \(A,D\) and \(h\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(B\), giving an exact argument.

    [3]

  3. Find the horizontal-axis intercept and sketch the curve.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The asymptotes give \(D-A=-2\) and \(D+A=6\). Adding yields \(D=2\), then \(A=4\). The centre has horizontal coordinate \(h\), so \(h=1\).

(b)

Substitute the point:

\[\frac{26}{5}=4\tanh\left(\frac B2\ln3\right)+2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\tanh\left(\frac B2\ln3\right)=\frac45.\]

The exponential definition gives \(\tanh(\ln3)=(9-1)/(9+1)=4/5\). Since tanh is one-to-one, \(\frac B2\ln3=\ln3\), so \(B=2\).

(c)

Set \(y=0\). Then \(\tanh(2(x-1))=-1/2\), so \(2(x-1)=-\tfrac12\ln3\). This gives \(x=1-\tfrac14\ln3\). Draw an increasing curve centred at \((1,2)\), through the given point and intercept, approaching \(-2\) on the left and 6 on the right.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The asymptotes have heights \(D-A\) and \(D+A\).

(b)

Find the tanh value at the given point and use \(\tanh(\ln3)=4/5\).

(c)

Solve \(\tanh(2(x-1))=-1/2\).

questions.title: An addition identity and exact evaluation
questions.prompt_html:
1. Starting from exponential definitions, prove \(\cosh(u+v)=\cosh u\cosh v+\sinh u\sinh v\).

    [4]

  2. Use this identity to evaluate \(\cosh(\ln2+\ln3)\) from the separate values at \(\ln2\) and \(\ln3\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Substitution into the right-hand side gives

\[\frac14\big[(e^u+e^{-u})(e^v+e^{-v})+(e^u-e^{-u})(e^v-e^{-v})\big].\]

Expanding, the terms \(e^{u-v}\) and \(e^{-u+v}\) cancel, leaving

\[\frac14(2e^{u+v}+2e^{-u-v})=\frac12(e^{u+v}+e^{-(u+v)})=\cosh(u+v).\]

No restrictions on the real numbers \(u,v\) were needed.

(b)

The four needed values are \(\cosh\ln2=5/4\), \(\sinh\ln2=3/4\), \(\cosh\ln3=5/3\), \(\sinh\ln3=4/3\). Hence

\[\cosh(\ln2+\ln3)=\frac54\frac53+\frac34\frac43=\frac{25+12}{12}=\frac{37}{12}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the two products on the right before adding.

(b)

Find each sinh and cosh from its exponential definition.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the four correct values in the addition identity.

questions.title: A double-angle equation for tanh
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove that \(\tanh2x=\frac{2\tanh x}{1+\tanh^2x}\).

    [3]

  2. Hence solve \(\tanh2x=\frac32\tanh x\), giving every real solution in logarithmic form.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Using \(\sinh2x=2\sinh x\cosh x\) and \(\cosh2x=\cosh^2x+\sinh^2x\),

\[\tanh2x=\frac{2\sinh x\cosh x}{\cosh^2x+\sinh^2x}=\frac{2\tanh x}{1+\tanh^2x}.\]

Division by \(\cosh^2x\) is valid for all real \(x\).

(b)

Put \(t=\tanh x\), so \(-1<t<1\). Then

\[\frac{2t}{1+t^2}=\frac32t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t(1-3t^2)=0.\]

Thus \(t=0\) or \(t=\pm1/\sqrt3\); all three are within the range of tanh. Since tanh is one-to-one,

\[x=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=\pm\frac12\ln\frac{\sqrt3+1}{\sqrt3-1}=\pm\frac12\ln(2+\sqrt3).\]

Keeping the factor \(t\) ensures that the solution \(x=0\) is not lost.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the double-angle formulae for sinh and cosh, then divide by \(\cosh^2x\).

(b)

Do not cancel \(\tanh x\) before checking whether it is zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Divide numerator and denominator by cosh squared.
Obtain and factor the cubic in t.

questions.title: A half-angle quotient
questions.prompt_html:
1. For \(x\ne0\), prove \(\frac{\cosh x+1}{\sinh x}=\operatorname{coth}\frac x2\).

    [3]

  2. Hence solve \(\frac{\cosh x+1}{\sinh x}=3\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The double-angle identities give

\[\cosh x+1=2\cosh^2\frac x2,\qquad \sinh x=2\sinh\frac x2\cosh\frac x2.\]

Therefore their quotient is \(\cosh(x/2)/\sinh(x/2)=\operatorname{coth}(x/2)\). The restriction \(x\ne0\) ensures the denominator is nonzero.

(b)

Part (a) gives \(\operatorname{coth}(x/2)=3\). Hence

\[\frac{e^x+1}{e^x-1}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^x+1=3e^x-3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^x=2.\]

Thus \(x=\ln2\), which is nonzero and satisfies the original equation.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Express the numerator and denominator using half-arguments.

(b)

Convert coth of the half-argument into an expression involving \(e^x\).

questions.title: A triple-angle identity for cosh
questions.prompt_html:
1. Starting from exponential definitions, prove \(\cosh3x=4\cosh^3x-3\cosh x\).

    [4]

  2. Hence solve \(\cosh3x=5\cosh x\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(u=e^x\), so \(u>0\). Then

\[4\cosh^3x-3\cosh x=\frac12(u+u^{-1})^3-\frac32(u+u^{-1}).\]

Since \((u+u^{-1})^3=u^3+3u+3u^{-1}+u^{-3}\), the linear terms cancel. The remaining expression is

\[\frac12(u^3+u^{-3})=\cosh3x.\]

(b)

The equation becomes \(4\cosh^3x-8\cosh x=0\). Because \(\cosh x>0\), division gives \(\cosh^2x=2\). Only \(\cosh x=\sqrt2\) is possible. Therefore

\[x=\pm\cosh^{-1}\sqrt2=\pm\ln(1+\sqrt2).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the cube of \((e^x+e^{-x})/2\).

(b)

Use \(\cosh x>0\) before dividing.

questions.title: Fourth powers that cancel
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove \(\cosh^4x-\sinh^4x=\cosh2x\).

    [2]

  2. Hence solve \(\cosh^4(2x)-\sinh^4(2x)=\frac{17}{8}\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Factor the left-hand side:

\[\cosh^4x-\sinh^4x=(\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x)(\cosh^2x+\sinh^2x).\]

The first factor is 1 and the second is \(\cosh2x\), which proves the result.

(b)

Applying part (a) to \(2x\) gives \(\cosh4x=17/8\). Now \(\cosh(\ln4)=(4+1/4)/2=17/8\), so \(4x=\pm\ln4\). Thus \(x=\pm\tfrac12\ln2\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor as a difference of two squares.

(b)

Apply the identity at argument \(2x\), not \(x\).

questions.title: A difference identity and monotonicity
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove that \(\tanh(x+a)-\tanh x=\frac{\sinh a}{\cosh(x+a)\cosh x}\). Hence explain why tanh is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb R\).

    [4]

  2. Given \(\tanh u=\frac13\) and \(\tanh v=\frac12\), find \(\tanh(u+v)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The displayed identity holds; if \(a>0\), its right-hand side is positive.

(b)

\(\tanh(u+v)=\frac57\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Combining the two fractions gives numerator

\[\sinh(x+a)\cosh x-\sinh x\cosh(x+a)=\sinh a.\]

The denominator is \(\cosh(x+a)\cosh x>0\), proving the identity. For any \(a>0\), \(\sinh a>0\), so \(\tanh(x+a)>\tanh x\). Any larger real argument can be written as \(x+a\) with \(a>0\); therefore tanh is strictly increasing everywhere.

(b)

The addition formula is

\[\tanh(u+v)=\frac{\tanh u+\tanh v}{1+\tanh u\tanh v}=\frac{1/3+1/2}{1+1/6}=\frac57.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Combine the fractions and use the sinh subtraction identity.

(b)

Divide the addition formula for sinh by that for cosh.

marking_criteria.description_html: Positive numerator and denominator when a is positive.
Conclude strict increase for all real arguments.

questions.title: An inadmissible quadratic root
questions.prompt_html:
1. Solve \(2\sinh^2x-5\cosh x+1=0\), giving all real solutions in exact logarithmic form.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cosh x\ge1\). The equation becomes

\[2(c^2-1)-5c+1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2c^2-5c-1=0.\]

Hence \(c=(5\pm\sqrt{33})/4\). The minus sign gives a negative value and must be rejected. Let \(C=(5+\sqrt{33})/4>1\). The equation \(\cosh x=C\) has the two solutions

\[x=\pm\cosh^{-1}C=\pm\ln(C+\sqrt{C^2-1}).\]

Both solve the original equation; there are no others.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\sinh^2x=\cosh^2x-1\), and remember \(\cosh x\ge1\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Reject the inadmissible root using the range of cosh.

questions.title: Keeping the zero solution
questions.prompt_html:
1. Solve \(\cosh2x=4\sinh x+1\) for real \(x\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Substitute the identity:

\[1+2\sinh^2x=4\sinh x+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2\sinh x(\sinh x-2)=0.\]

Thus \(\sinh x=0\) or \(\sinh x=2\). Since sinh is one-to-one on \(\mathbb R\), the solutions are \(x=0\) and \(x=\sinh^{-1}2=\ln(2+\sqrt5)\). Cancelling \(\sinh x\) at the start would incorrectly lose \(x=0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\cosh2x=1+2\sinh^2x\) and factor without cancelling sinh.

questions.title: Reciprocals and a nonzero domain
questions.prompt_html:
1. For \(x\ne0\), prove \(\operatorname{coth}x-\tanh x=2\operatorname{cosech}2x\).

    [3]

  2. Solve \(\operatorname{coth}x=5\tanh x\), in exact form.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\operatorname{coth}x-\tanh x=\frac{\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x}{\sinh x\cosh x}=\frac1{\sinh x\cosh x}=\frac2{\sinh2x}.\]

The fundamental and double-angle identities justify the last two steps. Every denominator is nonzero on the stated domain.

(b)

With \(t=\tanh x\ne0\), the equation is \(1/t=5t\), so \(t=\pm1/\sqrt5\). Both values are in \((-1,1)\) and are nonzero. Therefore

\[x=\pm\frac12\ln\frac{\sqrt5+1}{\sqrt5-1}=\pm\frac12\ln\left(\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\right).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Put the left-hand side over a common denominator.

(b)

Put \(t=\tanh x\ne0\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the double-angle identity with a valid domain.

questions.title: A shifted cosh and horizontal intersections
questions.prompt_html:
Define \(F(x)=5\cosh x-3\sinh x\), for all real \(x\).

  1. Show that \(F(x)=4\cosh(x-\ln2)\).

    [3]

  2. Determine the number of distinct real roots of \(F(x)=k\) for each real \(k\).

    [3]

  3. Find the roots when \(k=8\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(F(x)=4\cosh(x-\ln2)\).

(b)

Zero roots for \(k<4\); one for \(k=4\); two for \(k>4\).

(c)

\(x=\ln2\pm\ln(2+\sqrt3)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Since \(\cosh\ln2=5/4\) and \(\sinh\ln2=3/4\),

\[4\cosh(x-\ln2)=4\left(\cosh x\frac54-\sinh x\frac34\right)=5\cosh x-3\sinh x.\]

(b)

The range of \(F\) is \([4,\infty)\), with minimum 4 only at \(x=\ln2\). The function decreases to this point and then increases, symmetrically. Hence a horizontal line below 4 has no intersection, at 4 it has one, and above 4 it has two.

(c)

\(F(x)=8\) is equivalent to \(\cosh(x-\ln2)=2\). Thus \(x-\ln2=\pm\ln(2+\sqrt3)\), giving the two stated solutions.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the cosh subtraction identity and exact values at \(\ln2\).

(b)

Use the minimum of the shifted cosh graph.

(c)

Use \(\cosh^{-1}2=\ln(2+\sqrt3)\).

questions.title: Choosing the branch before inverting
questions.prompt_html:
The function \(f(x)=\cosh(2x-1)\) is to be restricted to a domain of the form \([a,\infty)\).

  1. Find the least value of \(a\) for which \(f\) is one-to-one, and state its range for this domain.

    [2]

  2. For this restriction, find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and state the domain and range of \(f^{-1}\).

    [3]

  3. Find \(f^{-1}(5/4)\) exactly.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The graph is symmetric about \(x=1/2\). If \(a<1/2\), the domain includes points on both sides of the minimum with the same value of cosh, so it is not one-to-one. On \([1/2,\infty)\) it is strictly increasing. Thus the least \(a\) is \(1/2\), and the range is \([1,\infty)\).

(b)

Write \(y=\cosh(2x-1)\), with \(2x-1\ge0\). The principal inverse gives \(2x-1=\cosh^{-1}y\). Therefore

\[f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1+\cosh^{-1}x}{2}.\]

The inverse domain is the original range \([1,\infty)\), and its range is the original restricted domain \([1/2,\infty)\).

(c)

Since the principal value \(\cosh^{-1}(5/4)=\ln2\), substitution yields \((1+\ln2)/2\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The minimum occurs when \(2x-1=0\).

(b)

The restricted argument \(2x-1\) is nonnegative.

(c)

\(\cosh(\ln2)=5/4\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Correct least endpoint with a branch explanation.

questions.title: Inverting a translated sinh function
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(f(x)=2\sinh(x-1)+3\), for \(x\in\mathbb R\).

  1. Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), stating its domain and range.

    [3]

  2. Solve \(f^{-1}(x)=1+\ln2\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

From \(y=2\sinh(x-1)+3\), obtain \(\sinh(x-1)=(y-3)/2\). Since sinh is one-to-one and has range \(\mathbb R\),

\[x=1+\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{y-3}{2}\right).\]

Interchanging the variable names gives the stated inverse. Both its domain and range are all real numbers.

(b)

\[\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x-3}{2}\right)=\ln2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac34.\]

Thus \(x=3+3/2=9/2\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Undo the vertical transformations before applying inverse sinh.

(b)

Apply \(f\) to both sides, or use the inverse formula.

questions.title: The domain of an inverse tanh transformation
questions.prompt_html:
Define \(f(x)=3\tanh(2x)+1\), for real \(x\).

  1. Find an expression for \(f^{-1}(x)\).

    [3]

  2. State the domain and range of \(f^{-1}\).

    [2]

  3. Solve \(f^{-1}(x)<0\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

If \(y=3\tanh(2x)+1\), then \(\tanh(2x)=(y-1)/3\). Applying the inverse gives \(2x=\tanh^{-1}((y-1)/3)\). Thus

\[f^{-1}(x)=\frac12\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{x-1}{3}\right).\]

(b)

The original range follows from \(-1<\tanh(2x)<1\): it is \(-2<f(x)<4\). This becomes the inverse domain. The original domain is all real numbers, so the inverse range is \(\mathbb R\).

(c)

Within the inverse domain, \(\tanh^{-1}((x-1)/3)<0\) precisely when \((x-1)/3<0\). Combining \(x<1\) with \(-2<x<4\) gives \(-2<x<1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Isolate tanh and remember to divide its argument by 2.

(b)

Tanh never attains either endpoint of its range.

(c)

Inverse tanh is increasing and is zero when its argument is zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply the inverse and rescale the argument.

questions.title: Compositions with inverse sinh
questions.prompt_html:
1. Simplify \(\sinh(\sinh^{-1}(3x-2))\) and \(\cosh(\sinh^{-1}x)\), stating the real domain of each expression.

    [3]

  2. Hence simplify \(\tanh(\sinh^{-1}x)\) and solve \(\tanh(\sinh^{-1}x)=\frac35\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(3x-2\) and \(\sqrt{1+x^2}\); both are defined for all real \(x\).

(b)

\(\tanh(\sinh^{-1}x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\); solution \(x=\frac34\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Sinh and its inverse are mutually inverse on \(\mathbb R\), so the first expression is \(3x-2\).

For the second, put \(u=\sinh^{-1}x\). Then \(\sinh u=x\), so \(\cosh^2u=1+x^2\). Since \(\cosh u>0\),

\[\cosh(\sinh^{-1}x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}.\]

Inverse sinh has all-real domain, so both expressions are defined for every real \(x\).

(b)

The quotient gives \(x/\sqrt{1+x^2}\). The equation forces \(x>0\). Squaring,

\[\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}=\frac9{25}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad16x^2=9.\]

Only \(x=3/4\) has the required positive sign. Direct substitution gives \((3/4)/(5/4)=3/5\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

For the second expression put \(u=\sinh^{-1}x\) and use the fundamental identity.

(b)

Use the quotient sinh/cosh, and check the sign before squaring.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the identity with the positive root for cosh.

questions.title: Why the principal inverse produces a modulus
questions.prompt_html:
1. Write \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh(2x-3))\) as a piecewise expression without hyperbolic functions.

    [3]

  2. Hence solve \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh(2x-3))=5\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Cosh is even. For a real \(u\), \(\cosh u=\cosh|u|\), and \(|u|\ge0\) lies on the principal inverse branch. Therefore \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh u)=|u|\), not necessarily \(u\). Taking \(u=2x-3\), the sign changes at \(x=3/2\), giving the stated piecewise formula.

(b)

The equation is \(|2x-3|=5\), so \(2x-3=5\) or \(2x-3=-5\). These give \(x=4\) and \(x=-1\). Both are admissible in the original all-real domain.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The principal inverse cosh returns a nonnegative value.

(b)

Solve both linear equations arising from the modulus.

questions.title: Inverse is not reciprocal
questions.prompt_html:
1. Simplify \(\tanh^{-1}(\tanh x)\) and \(\tanh(\tanh^{-1}x)\), stating the real domain of each composition. Explain why \(\tanh^{-1}x\) is not the same as \(\operatorname{coth}x\).

    [3]

  2. Solve \(\tanh^{-1}(2x)=\ln2\), checking the domain.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The first equals \(x\) for all real \(x\); the second equals \(x\) only for \(-1<x<1\). Coth is \(1/\tanh x\), not inverse tanh.

(b)

\(x=\frac3{10}\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Tanh maps \(\mathbb R\) bijectively onto \((-1,1)\). Thus applying inverse tanh after tanh gives the original real input. In the reverse order, the inner inverse tanh is defined only on \((-1,1)\), and on that domain the result is again \(x\).

The superscript \(-1\) in inverse-function notation means undoing a function. The reciprocal is \(1/\tanh x=\operatorname{coth}x\), defined for \(x\ne0\), and has a different domain and meaning.

(b)

The domain is \(-1/2<x<1/2\). Applying tanh,

\[2x=\tanh(\ln2)=\frac{4-1}{4+1}=\frac35.\]

Hence \(x=3/10\), which lies in the required domain.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Distinguish the inverse function from the reciprocal value.

(b)

First require \(-1<2x<1\).

questions.title: A translated inverse-sinh graph
questions.prompt_html:
A curve has equation \(y=\sinh^{-1}(x+1)-\ln2\).

  1. Sketch the curve. State its domain and range, its centre of symmetry, and its exact axis intercepts.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Inverse sinh is odd and strictly increasing, with all-real domain and range. The translations therefore give centre \((-1,-\ln2)\), with domain and range still \(\mathbb R\).

At a horizontal intercept, \(\sinh^{-1}(x+1)=\ln2\), so \(x+1=3/4\), giving \(x=-1/4\). At \(x=0\),

\[y=\sinh^{-1}1-\ln2=\ln\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}.\]

Sketch an increasing inverse-sinh curve through these points. Its slope flattens in both tails, but it has no horizontal asymptote: the outputs remain unbounded.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Start from the inverse-sinh graph, translate left by 1 and down by \(\ln2\).

questions.title: The endpoint of inverse cosh
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(y=\cosh^{-1}(x-2)\), using the principal inverse.

  1. State its domain and range, sketch the curve and describe its relationship to a suitable restricted cosh graph.

    [4]

  2. Find the point with \(y=\ln3\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Domain \([3,\infty)\); range \([0,\infty)\); endpoint \((3,0)\). It is the reflection of \(y=\cosh x+2\), \(x\ge0\), in \(y=x\).

(b)

\(\left(\frac{11}{3},\ln3\right)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The argument condition is \(x-2\ge1\), so \(x\ge3\). The principal inverse returns \(y\ge0\). At the endpoint, \(\cosh^{-1}1=0\), giving \((3,0)\).

Rearranging gives \(x=\cosh y+2\), with \(y\ge0\). Hence the graph is the reflection in \(y=x\) of \(y=\cosh x+2\) restricted to \(x\ge0\). It rises from the endpoint and becomes less steep as \(x\) increases.

(b)

\(\cosh^{-1}(x-2)=\ln3\) gives \(x-2=\cosh(\ln3)=5/3\). Thus \(x=11/3\), which is in the domain, and the point is \((11/3,\ln3)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Inverse cosh requires its argument to be at least 1.

(b)

Apply cosh to the equation.

questions.title: Deriving the logarithmic form of inverse sinh
questions.prompt_html:
1. Starting with \(y=\sinh^{-1}x\), derive a logarithmic expression for \(y\) and explain why it is valid for every real \(x\).

    [4]

  2. Hence solve \(\sinh^{-1}(2x-1)=\ln3\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

From \(x=\sinh y\),

\[2x=e^y-e^{-y}.\]

Let \(u=e^y>0\). Multiplication by \(u\) gives \(u^2-2xu-1=0\), so \(u=x\pm\sqrt{x^2+1}\). Since \(\sqrt{x^2+1}>|x|\), the plus choice is positive and the minus choice negative for every real \(x\). Therefore

\[y=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}).\]

The logarithm's argument is strictly positive for all real \(x\), establishing the domain as well as the branch.

(b)

Applying sinh gives \(2x-1=\sinh(\ln3)=4/3\). Hence \(2x=7/3\), so \(x=7/6\). There is no additional domain restriction.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Solve a quadratic in \(e^y\), which must be positive.

(b)

Exponentiate the derived expression, or apply sinh.

marking_criteria.description_html: Justify the unique positive choice for all x.

questions.title: Selecting the principal inverse-cosh branch
questions.prompt_html:
1. Derive \(\cosh^{-1}x=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})\), stating the domain and explaining the choice of sign.

    [4]

  2. Solve \(\cosh^{-1}(x+1)=\ln4\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Set \(y=\cosh^{-1}x\), where \(x\ge1\) and \(y\ge0\). Then \(2x=e^y+e^{-y}\). With \(u=e^y\ge1\),

\[u^2-2xu+1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=x\pm\sqrt{x^2-1}.\]

For \(x>1\), the two positive roots are reciprocals. The plus root exceeds 1 and the minus root is less than 1. The principal branch therefore requires the plus root. At \(x=1\), both give \(u=1\) and \(y=0\). Taking logarithms proves the formula on the whole domain.

(b)

The domain is \(x+1\ge1\), or \(x\ge0\). Applying cosh gives \(x+1=\cosh(\ln4)=17/8\), so \(x=9/8\). This satisfies the domain.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The principal inverse has \(y\ge0\), so \(e^y\ge1\).

(b)

The inverse requires \(x\ge0\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Use y nonnegative to justify the plus branch, including the endpoint.

questions.title: Inverse tanh: logarithm and graph
questions.prompt_html:
1. Derive a logarithmic expression for \(\tanh^{-1}x\) and state its real domain.

    [4]

  2. Sketch \(y=\tanh^{-1}x\), showing its asymptotes and intercept, and state its range and symmetry.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tanh^{-1}x=\frac12\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}\), for \(-1<x<1\).

(b)

Asymptotes \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\); intercept \((0,0)\); range \(\mathbb R\); odd symmetry.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(y=\tanh^{-1}x\). Using the exponential form,

\[x=\frac{e^{2y}-1}{e^{2y}+1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1-x)e^{2y}=1+x.\]

Hence

\[e^{2y}=\frac{1+x}{1-x},\qquad y=\frac12\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}.\]

Tanh has range \((-1,1)\), so this is the inverse domain. Equivalently, the exponential quotient is positive precisely on this interval. The endpoints are not allowed.

(b)

The logarithm tends to \(-\infty\) as \(x\to-1^+\) and to \(+\infty\) as \(x\to1^-\). Thus both asymptotes are vertical. The function is increasing, is zero at 0, and is odd because replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) reciprocates the logarithm's argument. Its range is all real numbers.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Express tanh using \(e^{2y}\), then solve for that exponential.

(b)

The graph is the reflection of \(y=\tanh x\) in \(y=x\).

questions.title: Exact inverse values with different forms
questions.prompt_html:
1. Solve \(\sinh^{-1}x+\sinh^{-1}\frac34=\sinh^{-1}\frac43\), giving a rational answer.

    [4]

  2. Show that this value of \(\sinh^{-1}x\) is also \(\tanh^{-1}(5/13)\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The logarithmic formula gives

\[\sinh^{-1}\frac34=\ln\left(\frac34+\frac54\right)=\ln2,\qquad \sinh^{-1}\frac43=\ln\left(\frac43+\frac53\right)=\ln3.\]

Consequently \(\sinh^{-1}x=\ln(3/2)\), so

\[x=\sinh\left(\ln\frac32\right)=\frac12\left(\frac32-\frac23\right)=\frac5{12}.\]

The one-to-one nature of inverse sinh ensures uniqueness.

(b)

\[\tanh^{-1}\frac5{13}=\frac12\ln\frac{18/13}{8/13}=\frac12\ln\frac94=\ln\frac32.\]

This is the inverse-sinh value obtained in part (a).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Evaluate the two constant inverse-sinh values using logarithms.

(b)

Use the logarithmic formula for inverse tanh.

questions.title: A sum of inverse tanh terms
questions.prompt_html:
1. Solve \(\tanh^{-1}x+\tanh^{-1}(2x)=\frac12\ln6\), giving all real solutions in exact form.

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Both inverse functions require \(-1/2<x<1/2\). On this interval all factors in the logarithmic expressions are positive, so

\[\ln\frac{(1+x)(1+2x)}{(1-x)(1-2x)}=\ln6.\]

The logarithm is one-to-one; hence

\[(1+x)(1+2x)=6(1-x)(1-2x).\]

Expansion gives \(10x^2-21x+5=0\), with roots \((21\pm\sqrt{241})/20\). The plus root exceeds \(1/2\) and is excluded. For the minus root, \(11<\sqrt{241}<21\), so it lies between 0 and \(1/2\). Thus

\[x=\frac{21-\sqrt{241}}{20}\]

is the only real solution. Every transformation used was reversible on the stated domain.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Find the common domain first. Combining the logarithms produces a quadratic, but not both roots are admissible.

marking_criteria.description_html: Reject the invalid root and give the valid exact solution.

questions.title: Three inverse functions, one value
questions.prompt_html:
1. For \(x\ge1\), prove \(\cosh^{-1}x=\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{x^2-1}=\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{x}\right)\).

    [4]

  2. Evaluate all three expressions when \(x=13/5\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

All three expressions equal the same nonnegative number \(u\).

(b)

Each expression equals \(\ln5\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(u=\cosh^{-1}x\ge0\). Then \(\cosh u=x\), and the fundamental identity gives \(\sinh u=\sqrt{x^2-1}\); the nonnegative root is needed because \(u\ge0\). Applying inverse sinh gives the first equality.

Also \(\tanh u=\sqrt{x^2-1}/x\). For finite \(x\ge1\), this ratio lies in \([0,1)\), the valid inverse-tanh domain. Applying inverse tanh gives the second equality. At \(x=1\), all expressions are zero, so the endpoint is included.

(b)

\[\cosh^{-1}\frac{13}{5}=\ln\left(\frac{13}{5}+\frac{12}{5}\right)=\ln5.\]

The other forms are \(\sinh^{-1}(12/5)=\ln5\) and \(\tanh^{-1}(12/13)=\tfrac12\ln25=\ln5\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Put \(u=\cosh^{-1}x\ge0\), then find sinh and tanh of \(u\).

(b)

\(\sqrt{(13/5)^2-1}=12/5\).

questions.title: A discriminant is not enough
questions.prompt_html:
For a real parameter \(k\), consider \(\cosh2x-k\cosh x+2=0\).

  1. With \(c=\cosh x\), reduce the equation to a quadratic and state the restriction on \(c\).

    [3]

  2. Determine the number of distinct real solutions in \(x\) for every real \(k\). Explain why a discriminant calculation alone is insufficient.

    [4]

  3. Find all real solutions when \(k=5\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(2c^2-kc+1=0\), with \(c\ge1\).

(b)

No solutions if \(k<3\); one if \(k=3\); two if \(k>3\).

(c)

\(x=\pm\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{17}}4\right)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The identity \(\cosh2x=2\cosh^2x-1\) gives

\[2c^2-1-kc+2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad2c^2-kc+1=0.\]

Because \(c=\cosh x\), only roots with \(c\ge1\) can correspond to real \(x\).

(b)

For an admissible \(c\), rearrange to \(k=2c+1/c\). On \([1,\infty)\), this function increases strictly: for \(c_2>c_1\ge1\),

\[\left(2c_2+\frac1{c_2}\right)-\left(2c_1+\frac1{c_1}\right)=(c_2-c_1)\left(2-\frac1{c_1c_2}\right)>0.\]

Its value at 1 is 3 and it grows without bound. Thus \(k<3\) gives no admissible \(c\), \(k=3\) gives \(c=1\) and only \(x=0\), while \(k>3\) gives exactly one \(c>1\) and hence two opposite real \(x\)-values.

The discriminant \(k^2-8\) only decides whether the quadratic has real roots in \(c\); it does not impose \(c\ge1\) or count the two inverse-cosh branches.

(c)

The two quadratic roots are \((5\pm\sqrt{17})/4\). The smaller lies below 1; the larger exceeds 1. Therefore

\[x=\pm\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{17}}4\right).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The range of cosh must accompany the quadratic.

(b)

Rearrange the quadratic as \(k=2c+1/c\) for \(c\ge1\).

(c)

Only the larger quadratic root is at least 1.

questions.title: A rational hyperbolic substitution
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(t=\tanh(x/2)\), where \(x\) is real.

  1. Show that \(\sinh x=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}\) and \(\cosh x=\frac{1+t^2}{1-t^2}\). State the range of \(t\).

    [4]

  2. Use this substitution to solve \(3\cosh x-2\sinh x=4\), giving answers in logarithmic form.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The exponential form gives

\[t=\frac{e^x-1}{e^x+1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^x=\frac{1+t}{1-t}.\]

Also \(-1<t<1\), so the denominator and the exponential are positive. Therefore

\[\sinh x=\frac12\left(\frac{1+t}{1-t}-\frac{1-t}{1+t}\right)=\frac{2t}{1-t^2},\]
\[\cosh x=\frac12\left(\frac{1+t}{1-t}+\frac{1-t}{1+t}\right)=\frac{1+t^2}{1-t^2}.\]

(b)

Substitution gives

\[\frac{3(1+t^2)-4t}{1-t^2}=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad7t^2-4t-1=0.\]

Hence \(t=(2\pm\sqrt{11})/7\), and both lie in \((-1,1)\). Using \(e^x=(1+t)/(1-t)\),

\[e^x=\frac{9\pm\sqrt{11}}{5\mp\sqrt{11}}=4\pm\sqrt{11}.\]

Both are positive. Taking logarithms gives the stated two solutions.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

First solve \(t=(e^x-1)/(e^x+1)\) for \(e^x\).

(b)

Check both quadratic roots against \(-1<t<1\), then use \(e^x=(1+t)/(1-t)\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Recover the exponential in terms of t.

questions.title: An inverse-function equation with a radical
questions.prompt_html:
1. Solve \(\cosh^{-1}(x+2)=2\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{x}\), showing that no extraneous solution has been introduced.

    [4]

  2. More generally, determine all real \(a\) for which \(\cosh^{-1}(x+a)=2\sinh^{-1}\sqrt{x}\) has a real solution, and find the solution.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The square root requires \(x\ge0\), which also ensures \(x+2\ge1\). Both sides are nonnegative. Since cosh is one-to-one on \([0,\infty)\), the equation is equivalent to

\[x+2=\cosh\left(2\sinh^{-1}\sqrt x\right)=1+2x.\]

Thus \(x=1\). It lies in the domain. The identity \(\cosh(2u)=1+2\sinh^2u\) and the principal branches make the transformation reversible, so this solution is neither extraneous nor incomplete.

(b)

On the common domain \(x\ge0\) and \(x+a\ge1\), both sides remain nonnegative. Applying cosh yields \(x+a=1+2x\), hence \(x=a-1\). The first domain condition requires \(a\ge1\). For such \(a\), the second condition is also satisfied because \(x+a=2a-1\ge1\). Thus the condition is necessary and sufficient, and the solution is unique.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Both sides are nonnegative on their common real domain, so applying cosh is reversible there.

(b)

After applying cosh, also check both original domain requirements.

marking_criteria.description_html: Necessary and sufficient parameter condition with uniqueness.

questions.title: Challenge: a complete parameter classification
questions.prompt_html:
For real \(a\), define \(F_a(x)=\cosh x-a\sinh x\) on \(\mathbb R\).

  1. For \(|a|<1\), write \(F_a(x)\) as \(R\cosh(x-b)\), where \(R>0\), and determine its minimum.

    [4]

  2. For every pair of real numbers \(a,k\), determine the number of distinct real solutions of \(F_a(x)=k\). Include \(a=1\) and \(a=-1\).

    [5]

  3. Find all solutions when \(a=3/5\) and \(k=1\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(R=\sqrt{1-a^2}\), \(b=\tanh^{-1}a\). The minimum is \(\sqrt{1-a^2}\), at \(x=\tanh^{-1}a\).

(b)

For \(|a|<1\), there are 0, 1 or 2 solutions according as \(k<\sqrt{1-a^2}\), \(k=\sqrt{1-a^2}\), or \(k>\sqrt{1-a^2}\).

For \(|a|=1\), there is one solution when \(k>0\) and none when \(k\le0\).

For \(|a|>1\), there is exactly one solution for every real \(k\).

(c)

\(x=0\) or \(x=\ln4\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Expanding gives \(R\cosh b=1\) and \(R\sinh b=a\). Subtracting their squares yields \(R^2=1-a^2\), so \(R=\sqrt{1-a^2}>0\). Taking their ratio gives \(\tanh b=a\), hence \(b=\tanh^{-1}a\). Therefore

\[F_a(x)=\sqrt{1-a^2}\cosh(x-\tanh^{-1}a).\]

Its minimum is \(\sqrt{1-a^2}\), occurring only when \(x=\tanh^{-1}a\).

(b)

For \(|a|<1\), part (a) gives the three cases from the minimum of a shifted cosh curve.

If \(a=1\), \(F_a=e^{-x}\); if \(a=-1\), \(F_a=e^x\). Each is one-to-one with range \((0,\infty)\), so each gives one solution for \(k>0\) and none otherwise.

If \(a>1\), the coefficient of \(e^x\) is negative and that of \(e^{-x}\) positive. Both terms decrease strictly as \(x\) increases. Their sum tends to \(+\infty\) on the left and \(-\infty\) on the right. Continuity and strict decrease therefore give exactly one solution at every height. If \(a<-1\), both terms instead increase strictly and the limits are reversed, with the same one-solution conclusion. This includes all real \(a,k\).

For completeness, when \(|a|<1\), the number of distinct real roots is

\[\begin{cases}0,&k<\sqrt{1-a^2},\\1,&k=\sqrt{1-a^2},\\2,&k>\sqrt{1-a^2}.\end{cases}\]

(c)

With \(u=e^x>0\), the equation is \(u/5+4/(5u)=1\), or \(u^2-5u+4=0\). Thus \(u=1,4\), giving \(x=0,\ln4\). As a check, the minimum is \(4/5<1\), so two roots are expected.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Compare \(R\cosh b\) and \(R\sinh b\) with 1 and \(a\).

(b)

For the remaining cases use \(F_a(x)=\frac{1-a}{2}e^x+\frac{1+a}{2}e^{-x}\).

(c)

The exponential equation factorises.

marking_criteria.description_html: All three cases for absolute a below 1.
Both boundary parameter cases and their ranges.
Use the exponential coefficients for absolute a above 1.
Complete one-solution classification for absolute a above 1.

questions.title: Two positive roots and a limiting case
questions.prompt_html:
1. Using exponential definitions, prove \(\cosh2x=1+2\sinh^2x\).

    [3]

  2. Find all real values of \(k\) for which \(\cosh2x+2=k\sinh x\) has two distinct positive real roots.

    [4]

  3. When \(k=2\sqrt6\), find the single distinct real root.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[1+2\sinh^2x=1+\frac12(e^x-e^{-x})^2=1+\frac12(e^{2x}-2+e^{-2x})=\frac12(e^{2x}+e^{-2x})=\cosh2x.\]

(b)

Put \(s=\sinh x\). The equation becomes \(2s^2-ks+3=0\). Since sinh is strictly increasing and \(\sinh0=0\), positive \(x\)-roots correspond exactly to positive \(s\)-roots.

The discriminant is \(k^2-24\), the product of the roots is \(3/2>0\), and their sum is \(k/2\). Thus the roots are distinct when \(|k|>2\sqrt6\), and both are positive exactly when also \(k>0\). Combining these conditions gives \(k>2\sqrt6\).

(c)

The repeated quadratic root is \(s=k/4=\sqrt6/2\). It corresponds to the single distinct value \(x=\sinh^{-1}(\sqrt6/2)=\ln((\sqrt6+\sqrt{10})/2)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the square of \(e^x-e^{-x}\).

(b)

The quadratic roots must be both distinct and positive; a positive discriminant alone is not enough.

(c)

Use the repeated root of the quadratic in sinh.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use root sum and product with positivity of sinh.

questions.title: An inverse-cosh antiderivative in a shifted equation
questions.prompt_html:
In this question \(x>3\).

  1. For \(u>4\), show that \(F(u)=\frac u2\sqrt{u^2-16}-8\cosh^{-1}(u/4)\) satisfies \(F^{\prime}(u)=\sqrt{u^2-16}\).

    [4]

  2. Solve \((x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}-y=2(x+1)^2\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}\), given that \(y=10\) when \(x=4\). Give an explicit exact expression for \(y\).

    [8]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The chain rule gives

\[\frac{d}{du}\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac u4\right)=\frac1{\sqrt{u^2-16}}.\]

By the product rule,

\[F^{\prime}(u)=\frac12\sqrt{u^2-16}+\frac{u^2}{2\sqrt{u^2-16}}-\frac8{\sqrt{u^2-16}}.\]

The last two terms combine to \((u^2-16)/(2\sqrt{u^2-16})\). Adding the first term yields \(\sqrt{u^2-16}\). The domain \(u>4\) ensures all derivative expressions are defined.

(b)

Divide by \(x+1>0\):

\[y^{\prime}-\frac{y}{x+1}=2(x+1)\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}.\]

An integrating factor is \(e^{-\int dx/(x+1)}=1/(x+1)\). Therefore

\[\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x+1}\right)=2\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}.\]

Putting \(u=x+1\) and using part (a),

\[\frac{y}{x+1}=(x+1)\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}-16\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+1}{4}\right)+C.\]

At \(x=4\), the radical is 3 and \(\cosh^{-1}(5/4)=\ln2\). The initial condition gives \(2=15-16\ln2+C\), so \(C=16\ln2-13\). Multiplication by \(x+1\) gives the stated explicit solution on \(x>3\). The initial point lies strictly inside this domain; the derivative identity is not asserted at its singular endpoint.

Final result

\(y=(x+1)\left[(x+1)\sqrt{(x+1)^2-16}-16\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+1}{4}\right)+16\ln2-13\right]\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate both terms before combining the fractions.

(b)

An integrating factor is \(1/(x+1)\). Then use part (a) with \(u=x+1\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Correct derivative of inverse cosh with its scale factor.

questions.title: Inverse sinh and a translated independent variable
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout this question \(x>-2\).

  1. Use integration by parts to find \(\int\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)\,dx\).

    [4]

  2. Solve \((x+2)y^{\prime}-y=(x+2)^2\sinh^{-1}((x+2)/3)\), given \(y=8\) when \(x=2\). Give your answer in the form \(y=f(x)\).

    [8]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Set \(u=x+2\). Integrating by parts gives

\[\int\sinh^{-1}(u/3)\,du=u\sinh^{-1}(u/3)-\int\frac{u}{\sqrt{u^2+9}}\,du.\]

The last integral is \(\sqrt{u^2+9}\), as is seen by the substitution \(v=u^2+9\). Thus

\[\int\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)dx=(x+2)\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)-\sqrt{(x+2)^2+9}+C.\]

(b)

Division by \(x+2\) puts the equation in linear form,

\[y^{\prime}-\frac{y}{x+2}=(x+2)\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right).\]

The integrating factor is \(1/(x+2)\), valid on the stated domain. Therefore

\[\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x+2}\right)=\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right).\]

Using part (a),

\[\frac{y}{x+2}=(x+2)\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)-\sqrt{(x+2)^2+9}+C.\]

When \(x=2\), \(\sinh^{-1}(4/3)=\ln3\) and the radical is 5. Hence \(2=4\ln3-5+C\), giving \(C=7-4\ln3\). Multiplying by \(x+2\) yields the required explicit solution.

Final result

\(y=(x+2)\left[(x+2)\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right)-\sqrt{(x+2)^2+9}+7-4\ln3\right]\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

First put \(u=x+2\). In the remaining integral, use \(d(\sinh^{-1}(u/3))/du=1/\sqrt{u^2+9}\).

(b)

Multiply the linear form by \(1/(x+2)\) and use part (a).

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the initial condition and exact inverse value.

questions.title: A coth integrating factor and an endpoint limit
questions.prompt_html:
In this question \(x>0\).

  1. Show that \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln(\operatorname{coth}x)=-2\operatorname{cosech}2x\).

    [3]

  2. Solve \(\sinh2x\,y^{\prime}-2y=\sinh2x\), given \(y=8/5\) when \(x=\ln3\).

    [6]

  3. Find \(\lim_{x\to0^+}y\).

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

On \(x>0\), coth is positive, so its logarithm is defined. Write

\[\ln(\operatorname{coth}x)=\ln(\cosh x)-\ln(\sinh x).\]

Differentiating gives \(\tanh x-\operatorname{coth}x=-1/(\sinh x\cosh x)=-2/\sinh2x\), as required.

(b)

The linear form is \(y^{\prime}-2\operatorname{cosech}2x\,y=1\). By part (a), an integrating factor is \(\operatorname{coth}x\). Hence

\[\frac d{dx}(y\operatorname{coth}x)=\operatorname{coth}x.\]

Integrating on \(x>0\) gives \(y\operatorname{coth}x=\ln(\sinh x)+C\). At \(x=\ln3\), \(\sinh x=4/3\) and \(\operatorname{coth}x=5/4\), so \((8/5)(5/4)=\ln(4/3)+C\). Thus \(C=2-\ln(4/3)\). Multiplication by \(\tanh x\) gives the answer.

Final result

\(y=\tanh x\left[\ln(\sinh x)+2-\ln\frac43\right]\).

(c)

As \(x\to0^+\), \(\tanh x/x\to1\) and \(\sinh x/x\to1\). Thus

\[\tanh x\ln(\sinh x)=\frac{\tanh x}{x}\left[x\ln x+x\ln\left(\frac{\sinh x}{x}\right)\right]\to0.\]

The constant term multiplied by tanh also tends to zero. Therefore the limit is 0. This is a one-sided limit, not an assertion that the solution extends to a differentiable solution through \(x=0\); the problem is posed on \(x>0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(\operatorname{coth}x=\cosh x/\sinh x\).

(b)

Part (a) identifies the integrating factor after division by \(\sinh2x\).

(c)

The logarithm diverges, but it is multiplied by a factor tending to zero.

questions.title: A scaled identity and long-run behaviour
questions.prompt_html:
1. Use exponential definitions to prove \(2\cosh^2(2x)=\cosh4x+1\).

    [3]

  2. Solve \(y^{\prime}+4y\tanh(2x)=3\), given \(y=-1\) when \(x=0\).

    [6]

  3. Find \(\lim_{x\to\infty}y\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Using the definition of cosh,

\[2\cosh^2(2x)=\frac12(e^{2x}+e^{-2x})^2=\frac12(e^{4x}+2+e^{-4x})=\cosh4x+1.\]

(b)

An integrating factor is

\[\exp\left(\int4\tanh(2x)dx\right)=\exp(2\ln\cosh2x)=\cosh^2(2x).\]

Thus \(\frac d{dx}(y\cosh^2(2x))=3\cosh^2(2x)\). Using part (a),

\[y\cosh^2(2x)=\frac32\int(\cosh4x+1)dx=\frac38\sinh4x+\frac32x+C.\]

At \(x=0\), the initial condition gives \(C=-1\). Dividing by the positive \(\cosh^2(2x)\) yields the stated solution, valid for all real \(x\).

Final result

\(y=\operatorname{sech}^2(2x)\left[\frac38\sinh4x+\frac32x-1\right]\).

(c)

Rewrite the solution as

\[y=\frac34\tanh2x+\left(\frac32x-1\right)\operatorname{sech}^2(2x).\]

The first term tends to \(3/4\). The second tends to zero because the reciprocal cosh-squared factor decays exponentially, faster than the linear factor grows. Hence the limit is \(3/4\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the square of \((e^{2x}+e^{-2x})/2\).

(b)

The integrating factor is \(\cosh^2(2x)\).

(c)

Use \(\sinh4x=2\sinh2x\cosh2x\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Separate the bounded tanh term from the decaying term.

questions.title: Challenge: from a triple-angle identity to a differential equation
questions.prompt_html:
1. Prove from exponential definitions that \(\sinh3x=3\sinh x+4\sinh^3x\).

    [4]

  2. Use \(u=\sinh x\) to find \(\int\sinh^2(3x)\cosh x\,dx\).

    [4]

  3. Hence solve \(y^{\prime}+y\tanh x=\sinh^2(3x)\), given \(y=2\) when \(x=0\).

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(u=e^x\). Then

\[3\sinh x+4\sinh^3x=\frac32(u-u^{-1})+\frac12(u-u^{-1})^3.\]

The cubic expansion is \(u^3-3u+3u^{-1}-u^{-3}\). The linear terms cancel, leaving \(\frac12(u^3-u^{-3})=\sinh3x\), proving the result.

(b)

With \(u=\sinh x\), \(du=\cosh x\,dx\), and part (a) gives \(\sinh3x=3u+4u^3\). Thus

\[\int\sinh^2(3x)\cosh x\,dx=\int(3u+4u^3)^2du=\int(9u^2+24u^4+16u^6)du.\]

Term-by-term integration gives \(3u^3+(24/5)u^5+(16/7)u^7+C\). Substituting back gives the stated antiderivative.

Final result

\(3\sinh^3x+\frac{24}{5}\sinh^5x+\frac{16}{7}\sinh^7x+C\).

(c)

The integrating factor is \(e^{\int\tanh x dx}=\cosh x\). Multiplication gives

\[\frac d{dx}(y\cosh x)=\sinh^2(3x)\cosh x.\]

Use part (b) to obtain

\[y\cosh x=3\sinh^3x+\frac{24}{5}\sinh^5x+\frac{16}{7}\sinh^7x+C.\]

At \(x=0\), \(\cosh0=1\) and \(\sinh0=0\), so \(C=2\). Divide by \(\cosh x>0\) to obtain the required solution for every real \(x\). Differentiating the product \(y\cosh x\) also gives a direct check of the equation.

Final result

\(y=\operatorname{sech}x\left[3\sinh^3x+\frac{24}{5}\sinh^5x+\frac{16}{7}\sinh^7x+2\right]\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand \((e^x-e^{-x})^3\) and combine with the linear term.

(b)

Part (a) makes the transformed integrand a polynomial in \(u\).

(c)

Multiply by \(\cosh x\).
